DECISION before building -- `position` as a panel word. Two values ship: `static` (in flow, today) and `absolute` (out of flow, over its slot). `fixed` and `sticky` are REJECTED, both by measurement, not by argument. FIXED: an abspos probe inside .panel-items and inside .panel-workspace both resolve to the workspace's own box (900x400 measured), but the same probe set to `fixed` resolves to the VIEWPORT (1600x1000) from both places -- container-type: size is a containing block for absolutely positioned descendants and not for fixed ones. So a fixed panel leaves the workspace and lands over the site chrome. Never right for an embedded design tool. STICKY: walked the overflow chain up from a .panel -- .panel (hidden, scrollW==clientW), .panel-workspace (visible), .bleed (visible), .default flow (visible), then .pages, the SITE's page scroller, scrollH 7129 vs clientH 900. Nothing between a panel and there ever scrolls. A sticky panel would therefore stick to the browser viewport as the HOST PAGE scrolls, clamped inside .panel-items -- inert in a full-height workspace, and in an embedded one its behaviour is a property of the page it was embedded in rather than of the panel. That is not a panel word.

DECISION part 2 -- WHY absolute is safe here, and how Mike's answer lands. The containing block is bounded on both paths and neither was assumed: a nested panel's is its parent split's .panel-items, which insert.css already makes position: relative (measured 900x400 = the row); a root leaf's is .panel-workspace, a size query container and therefore a containing block for abspos (measured 900x400, not the viewport). So a floating panel can never escape the workspace and no panel.css change is needed. THE COLLAPSE, MEASURED: forcing a middle panel to position:absolute today with no support gives a 0x0 box -- the container-type trap again, a shrink-to-fit box whose contained body reports empty -- and its two grips land on the SAME x (450, 450), one seam drawn twice with the top one resizing a panel that occupies nothing. Mike's answer is the fix and it is the mechanism this file already owns: a DECLARED extent capped against the slot. fill -> inset 0 that axis; hug -> min(var(--panel-hug), 100%); fixed -> min(var(--panel-w-at), 100%). Measured that % on an abspos box resolves against the containing block and never against itself (min(600px,100%) -> 400 in a 400px CB), so min(x, 100%) is exactly right here and there is no self-measuring loop.

DECISION part 3 -- derived, not seeded; and self needs NO new machinery. Two ways to keep a floating panel from collapsing: measure its rect in JS and write w_at/h_at on the way out of flow, or let the CSS give every extent a declared value capped against the containing block. The second wins -- no data written behind the user's back, no number that is stale the moment the slot changes, idempotent, and CONTINUOUS: a floating panel reads the same w/h extents and the same --panel-self-x/-y it already had, so switching modes moves nothing except the siblings, which is precisely what float means. And measured: Chrome honours justify-self/align-self on an absolutely positioned box whose insets are 0 (justify-self: center on a 100px box in a 400px CB lands at +150; align-self: end on a 50px box in a 300px CB lands at 250). So the two custom properties sizing() already writes unconditionally do the whole placement job, and the indirection that landed an hour ago is untouched -- the floating rules are simply another set gated on a NON-filling axis, for the same reason: alignment other than normal/stretch makes an abspos box shrink-to-fit, so justify-self on a filling axis would be the collapse itself.
